title: Roman and Civil Law Foundations
topics: Sources and institutions of Roman law

notes.h: Sources and institutions of Roman law
notes.body:
Roman law developed over more than a thousand years, from the Twelve Tables to Justinian's codification and beyond. A good answer places each source in its period.

Periods
- Archaic (to about 250 BC): the Twelve Tables (traditionally 451–450 BC) and the pontiffs' monopoly of legal knowledge.
- Pre-classical and classical (about 250 BC to AD 235): the praetor's edict and the great jurists. The classical period is usually dated from Augustus to the end of the Severan dynasty.
- Post-classical (to AD 527): imperial legislation dominates, leading to the Theodosian Code (AD 438).
- Justinianic (527–565): the Corpus Iuris Civilis.

Sources of law (Gaius, Institutes 1.2)
- leges, passed by assemblies, such as the lex Aquilia (traditionally 287 BC)
- plebiscita, resolutions of the plebeian assembly, binding on all after the lex Hortensia (287 BC)
- senatus consulta, which gained the force of law in the early Empire
- imperial constitutions: edicts, decrees, rescripts and mandates
- magistrates' edicts, especially the praetor's
- responsa prudentium, opinions of jurists; Augustus gave some jurists the ius respondendi

The praetor
The urban praetor (from 367 BC) and the peregrine praetor (from 242 BC) published an annual edict listing the remedies they would grant. The praetor could not make civil law, but he could aid, supplement or correct it (Papinian, D.1.1.7.1). This produced ius honorarium, which developed new actions, defences (exceptiones) and bonorum possessio. Under Hadrian the jurist Julian consolidated the edict in about AD 130.

Procedure
- legis actiones: rigid oral forms; one wrong word could lose the case
- the formulary system: the praetor drafted a written formula naming the issue for a lay judge (iudex). It was introduced by the lex Aebutia (2nd century BC) and made general by Augustus's leges Iuliae.
- cognitio extraordinaria: an official heard the whole case, with appeal; this became the norm in the later Empire.

Jurists and the Corpus Iuris Civilis
The classical jurists include Labeo and Capito, the Sabinian and Proculian schools, Julian, Gaius, Papinian, Paul and Ulpian. The Law of Citations (AD 426) told courts to follow Papinian, Paul, Gaius, Ulpian and Modestinus. Justinian's commission, led by Tribonian, produced:
- the Code (529, revised 534)
- the Digest or Pandects (533), 50 books of excerpted juristic writings
- the Institutes (533), a student textbook modelled on Gaius
- the Novels, Justinian's later legislation

Exam pitfalls:
- Gaius's Institutes survive largely from a palimpsest found in Verona in 1816; much of our knowledge of classical law depends on it.
- Justinian's compilers altered texts (interpolations); be cautious when treating Digest passages as purely classical.
- The praetor did not legislate in the strict sense; he granted or refused remedies.

The law of persons (G.1.8) deals with status: whether one is free, a citizen, and independent.

Freedom: slaves and freedmen
- Slaves were legally things (res) and owners had broad powers, though later imperial law restricted cruelty; Antoninus Pius allowed abused slaves to seek sale.
- Slaves could hold a peculium, a fund the master allowed them to manage. Third parties could sue the master up to the value of the peculium (actio de peculio).
- Manumission by vindicta (before a magistrate), by census or by will made the slave a citizen if the owner was a citizen. Informal manumission gave only the lesser status of Junian Latin.
- The lex Fufia Caninia (2 BC) capped manumissions by will; the lex Aelia Sentia (AD 4) set minimum ages (slave 30, master 20).
- Freedmen owed obsequium and operae to the patron, who also had rights in their estate.

Citizenship
Citizens enjoyed commercium and conubium. The Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212) of Caracalla granted citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.

Family: patria potestas
- The paterfamilias held power over his descendants through males, whatever their age, until his death or emancipation.
- In early law this included the power of life and death (ius vitae necisque), though this was rarely used and later curtailed.
- Children in potestate could own nothing in civil law; acquisitions went to the father. Over time sons gained the peculium castrense, property earned through military service.
- Potestas arose by birth in lawful marriage, adoption (of a person in power) or adrogation (of a person sui iuris).
- Emancipation used the Twelve Tables rule that a father who sold his son three times lost potestas.

Marriage
- Classical marriage required consent, capacity and conubium. It was usually without manus, so the wife stayed in her father's power or was sui iuris, and property stayed separate.
- Marriage with manus (by confarreatio, coemptio or usus) was rare by the classical period.
- Divorce was free to either spouse; gifts between spouses were void; the dowry (dos) was returnable on divorce, subject to retentions.

Guardianship
Tutela covered impuberes (boys under 14, girls under 12) and in early law all women sui iuris (tutela mulierum), which had weakened greatly by Gaius's time. Cura protected those over puberty but under 25 (after the lex Plaetoria), the insane and spendthrifts.

Worked example: Marcus, aged 30, lives with his father Lucius. He buys a farm. In classical law the farm belongs to Lucius, because Marcus is in potestas, unless it forms part of his peculium castrense.

Exam pitfalls:
- Age of majority did not end potestas; only the father's death, emancipation or certain offices did.

Roman law distinguished ownership (dominium) from possession, and classified things carefully.

Classification of things
- res in patrimonio and res extra patrimonium (sacred, religious, public and common things such as the air and sea)
- res corporales and res incorporales (rights such as servitudes and debts) (G.2.12–14)
- res mancipi (Italian land, slaves, oxen, horses, mules and donkeys, and rustic praedial servitudes) and res nec mancipi. Justinian abolished the distinction in 531.

Transfer of ownership
- mancipatio: a formal ceremony with scales, five witnesses and a scale-holder, required for res mancipi
- in iure cessio: a collusive claim before the magistrate
- traditio: delivery with intention to transfer, sufficient for res nec mancipi; in Justinian's law the general method. A iusta causa is required.
If a res mancipi was only delivered, the transferee had bonitary ownership, protected by the praetor (actio Publiciana and exceptio rei venditae et traditae), and could become full owner by usucapion.

Original acquisition
- Occupatio: taking an ownerless thing. Wild animals belong to the captor until they regain their natural freedom; Justinian's Institutes say a wounded animal belongs to the hunter only when caught (J.2.1.13).
- Accessio: the lesser thing accedes to the greater; superficies solo cedit (buildings belong to the land owner).
- Specificatio: making a new thing from another's material. The Sabinians gave it to the material's owner; the Proculians to the maker. Justinian's middle view: if it can be reduced to its material, the material owner takes; otherwise the maker.
- Fruits belong to the owner, but a good faith possessor acquires them on separation.
- Treasure: Hadrian's rule gave treasure found on one's own land to the finder, and divided treasure found by chance on another's land equally between the finder and the landowner.

Usucapio
Ownership acquired by possession over time. The Twelve Tables set one year for movables and two for land. Requirements became: res habilis (not stolen or taken by force), iusta causa (titulus), good faith at the start, and possession for the period. Justinian merged usucapio with longi temporis praescriptio: three years for movables, ten or twenty for land.

Possession and remedies
- Possession requires corpus (physical control) and animus (intention to hold as one's own). Tenants and borrowers had only detention.
- Possessory interdicts protected possession regardless of title, for example uti possidetis for land and utrubi for movables, and unde vi for violent dispossession.
- Ownership was protected by the rei vindicatio.

Exam pitfalls:
- Stolen things could not be usucapted even by a good faith buyer.
- Possession is not ownership: a thief has possession protected by interdicts against third parties.

An obligation is a legal tie by which we are bound to perform something according to the law of our state (J.3.13 pr.). Gaius divided obligations into those arising from contract and from delict, plus a residual category later called 'various causes'. Justinian used four categories: contract, quasi-contract, delict and quasi-delict.

Roman law had no general law of contract; it recognised specific contracts, which Gaius grouped by how they arose (G.3.89).

Real contracts (re): formed by delivery of a thing
- mutuum: loan for consumption, such as money; the borrower returns the same quantity and quality
- commodatum: gratuitous loan for use; the borrower returns the same thing and is liable for custodia
- depositum: gratuitous safekeeping; the depositee is liable only for dolus and gross negligence
- pignus: pledge as security

Verbal contracts (verbis)
The stipulatio: an oral question and matching answer ('Do you promise?' 'I promise.'). It was abstract, enforceable regardless of purpose, and could give effect to any lawful promise. Later practice relied on written records of stipulation.

Literal contracts (litteris)
Entries in account books (nomina transcripticia), obsolete by Justinian's time.

Consensual contracts (consensu): formed by agreement alone, governed by good faith (bonae fidei)
- emptio venditio (sale): agreement on thing and price; risk passed to the buyer once the sale was perfecta (periculum est emptoris). The seller warranted against eviction and, through the aediles' edict, against latent defects in slaves and animals (actio redhibitoria, actio quanti minoris).
- locatio conductio (hire): of a thing, of services or of a piece of work
- societas (partnership)
- mandatum (gratuitous mandate)

Innominate contracts and pacts
Agreements such as exchange (permutatio) became enforceable once one party had performed (actio praescriptis verbis). Bare pacts generally gave no action: ex nudo pacto actio non nascitur. Some pacts were enforced by the praetor or added to good faith contracts.

Quasi-contract includes negotiorum gestio (management of another's affairs without mandate) and unjustified enrichment claims (condictiones, such as the condictio indebiti for payment of what was not due).

Worked example: Gaia sells a horse to Publius for 1,000 sesterces. Before delivery it is struck by lightning. The sale was perfect, so risk had passed and Publius must still pay, unless Gaia was at fault.

Exam pitfalls:
- The stipulatio was formal; consensual contracts were informal. Do not confuse their bases.
- Commodatum is gratuitous; a loan for use with payment is locatio conductio.
- Sale did not itself transfer ownership; delivery (traditio) did.

Gaius lists four delicts: furtum (theft), rapina (robbery with violence), damnum iniuria datum (wrongful loss) and iniuria (outrage to personality). Delictual actions were penal: they aimed at a penalty, were not transmissible against the heir, and could be brought against each of several wrongdoers in full.

The lex Aquilia (traditionally 287 BC) was a plebiscite with three chapters:
- Chapter 1: killing another's slave or four-footed herd animal (pecus). Damages equal the highest value it had in the year before.
- Chapter 2: fraudulent release of a debt by an adstipulator; obsolete.
- Chapter 3: other damage to property by burning, breaking or rending (urere, frangere, rumpere), with damages based on the value within 30 days, which the jurists read as the highest value in the 30 days before the wrong. The jurists read rumpere broadly as corrumpere, covering any spoiling.
Damages doubled against a defendant who denied liability (lis infitiando crescit in duplum).

Requirements
- damnum: financial loss to the owner, assessed by his interest (id quod interest), so consequential loss could count
- iniuria: unlawfulness, interpreted to require fault (culpa or dolus). Even the slightest fault sufficed (in lege Aquilia et levissima culpa venit, D.9.2.44 pr.)
- causation: originally direct physical killing or damage by the defendant's body to the thing (corpore corpori). Indirect causing gave an actio in factum or utilis.

Key texts on fault and causation
- The pruner case (D.9.2.31): a pruner dropping a branch on a passer-by is liable if he failed to shout a warning where people might pass. Paul adds that culpa exists where what a diligent person could foresee was not foreseen.
- The javelin case (D.9.2.9.4): a soldier practising on a training ground who hits a slave is not liable; one throwing in an unusual place is.
- The barber case (D.9.2.11 pr.): a barber shaving a slave next to a ball game; liability may fall on the player, but a person who chose to be shaved in a dangerous place has himself to blame.
- Killing an attacker in self-defence was not iniuria (D.9.2.45.4).

Extension
Praetorian actions extended liability to indirect causation (for example, shutting up an animal so it starves), to non-owners such as usufructuaries, and, according to Ulpian, to a free person who was injured (actio utilis, D.9.2.13 pr.).

Worked example: Rufus negligently leaves a gate open, and Sextus's horse escapes and is killed on the road. This is not killing corpore corpori, so Sextus would need an actio in factum rather than direct Aquilian action.

Exam pitfalls:
- Chapter 1 looks back one year, Chapter 3 thirty days.
- Iniuria under the lex Aquilia means unlawfulness or fault, not the separate delict of iniuria.

notes.h: The civil law tradition and comparison
notes.body:
The civil law tradition is the family of legal systems built on Roman law as received and rationalised in continental Europe.

Reception
- The Digest was rediscovered in Italy in the late 11th century. At Bologna, Irnerius and the Glossators wrote glosses explaining it; Accursius compiled the Glossa Ordinaria (about 1230).
- The Commentators (Post-glossators), such as Bartolus of Sassoferrato and Baldus de Ubaldis, adapted Roman law to contemporary needs in the 14th century.
- Roman law combined with canon law to form the ius commune, taught across European universities.
- Humanists (mos gallicus), including Cujas, studied Roman law historically. Natural lawyers such as Grotius and Pufendorf systematised it.
- The Roman-Dutch law of Grotius and Voet passed to South Africa, Sri Lanka and elsewhere.

Codification
- French Code civil (1804): Napoleonic, accessible, influenced by Domat and Pothier. Article 1240 (formerly 1382) is a general clause for fault liability; contract law was reformed in 2016.
- German BGB (in force 1900): built on the Pandectist science of Savigny and Windscheid, with an abstract General Part and the abstraction principle, separating the real agreement transferring ownership from the obligation to transfer. Delict liability in § 823 is based on protected interests rather than a general clause.
- Swiss Civil Code (1907) and Code of Obligations; later codes in Italy (1942), the Netherlands (1992) and elsewhere.

Comparison with common law
- Sources: civil law treats the code as the primary source, with judicial decisions persuasive in principle; in practice settled case law (jurisprudence constante) carries great weight. Common law treats precedent as binding (stare decisis).
- Method: civil law reasons from general principles downwards; common law reasons by analogy from cases.
- Substance: civil law has no consideration requirement and accepts specific performance as a primary remedy; English law requires consideration (or a deed) and treats damages as the primary remedy. Civil law generally lets third parties benefit from contracts (stipulation pour autrui); English law moved closer with the 1999 Act.
- Good faith: § 242 BGB imposes a general duty of good faith in performance; English law has no general duty (Walford v Miles [1992] 2 AC 128 rejected a duty to negotiate in good faith), though it recognises implied duties in some relational contracts.

Mixed systems: Scotland, South Africa, Louisiana and Quebec combine civilian and common law elements.

Exam pitfalls:
- Roman law influenced English law too, for example through Bracton, admiralty, and Holt CJ's use of Roman bailment categories in Coggs v Bernard (1703).
- Do not overstate the divide: civil law courts follow settled case law, and English law is heavily statutory.

cards.f: When were the Twelve Tables traditionally enacted?
cards.b: Around 451–450 BC, by a board of ten men (decemviri).

cards.f: Name the four parts of Justinian's Corpus Iuris Civilis.
cards.b: The Code, the Digest (Pandects), the Institutes and the Novels.

cards.f: When were the Digest and Institutes promulgated?
cards.b: AD 533; the revised Code followed in 534.

cards.f: What, according to Papinian, could the praetor do in relation to the civil law?
cards.b: He could aid, supplement or correct it for the public benefit (D.1.1.7.1), but not make civil law directly.

cards.f: What is ius honorarium?
cards.b: Law derived from magistrates' edicts, chiefly the praetor's, which created new actions, defences and remedies alongside the civil law.

cards.f: Who consolidated the praetor's edict, and when?
cards.b: The jurist Julian, under Hadrian, in about AD 130.

cards.f: Describe the formulary procedure.
cards.b: The praetor drafted a written formula framing the issue, and a lay judge (iudex) decided the facts and gave judgment; it replaced the rigid legis actiones.

cards.f: What was the ius respondendi?
cards.b: A privilege granted by Augustus and later emperors to certain jurists to give opinions with imperial authority.

cards.f: What was the Law of Citations (AD 426)?
cards.b: An imperial constitution directing courts to follow the opinions of Papinian, Paul, Gaius, Ulpian and Modestinus, with a majority rule and Papinian prevailing on a tie.

cards.f: Why do Romanists worry about interpolations?
cards.b: Justinian's compilers were authorised to alter classical texts, so some Digest passages reflect 6th-century law rather than classical law.

cards.f: How was Gaius's Institutes rediscovered?
cards.b: Through a palimpsest found in Verona in 1816, where the text lay under later writing.

cards.f: What is Gaius's threefold division of law?
cards.b: Law relating to persons, things and actions (G.1.8).

cards.f: What was a peculium?
cards.b: A fund or property that a master or father allowed a slave or son to manage; in law it belonged to the master or father.

cards.f: What was the actio de peculio?
cards.b: An action letting creditors of a slave or son in power sue the master or father up to the value of the peculium.

cards.f: Name three formal methods of manumission.
cards.b: By vindicta (before a magistrate), by census and by will.

cards.f: What did the lex Aelia Sentia (AD 4) require?
cards.b: Among other things, that a slave under 30 could not become a citizen on manumission, and that a master under 20 could not validly manumit, unless cause was shown before a council (and, for the slave, manumission was by vindicta).

cards.f: What did the Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212) do?
cards.b: Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to almost all free inhabitants of the empire.

cards.f: Did reaching adulthood end patria potestas?
cards.b: No. Potestas lasted until the father's death, emancipation, or certain events such as the child becoming a flamen dialis or Vestal Virgin.

cards.f: Distinguish adoption from adrogation.
cards.b: Adoption brought a person already in another's power into the adopter's potestas; adrogation brought a person sui iuris, with their own dependants and property, under potestas.

cards.f: What was the peculium castrense?
cards.b: Property earned through military service, which a son in power could hold and dispose of as if he were sui iuris.

cards.f: How did emancipation use the Twelve Tables?
cards.b: The Twelve Tables provided that a father who sold his son three times lost potestas; jurists used three fictitious sales (mancipationes) to free a son.

cards.f: What was marriage without manus?
cards.b: The usual classical form, in which the wife did not enter her husband's family or power, so property stayed separate.

cards.f: Who was subject to tutela impuberum?
cards.b: Children sui iuris below puberty: under 14 for boys, under 12 for girls.

cards.f: List the res mancipi.
cards.b: Italian land, slaves, oxen, horses, mules and donkeys, and rustic praedial servitudes.

cards.f: What was mancipatio?
cards.b: A formal transfer for res mancipi, with five citizen witnesses, a scale-holder, a bronze ingot and scales.

cards.f: What is traditio and what did it require?
cards.b: Delivery of a thing with intention to transfer ownership, based on a recognised justifying cause (iusta causa); it sufficed for res nec mancipi.

cards.f: What was bonitary ownership?
cards.b: Praetorian protection for a person who received a res mancipi by mere delivery, until usucapion made them full civil-law owner.

cards.f: What are the classical requirements of usucapio?
cards.b: A thing capable of usucapion, iusta causa, good faith at the start of possession, and possession for the required period.

cards.f: What were the Twelve Tables periods for usucapion?
cards.b: One year for movables and two years for land.

cards.f: State Justinian's middle view on specificatio.
cards.b: If the new thing can be reduced to its original material, it belongs to the owner of the material; if not, it belongs to the maker (who in good faith used another's material).

cards.f: What does superficies solo cedit mean?
cards.b: Whatever is built on land accedes to the land and belongs to the landowner.

cards.f: When does a hunter acquire a wounded wild animal under Justinian's Institutes?
cards.b: Only on capture, not merely by wounding it (J.2.1.13).

cards.f: Why could a good faith buyer of a stolen horse not usucapt it?
cards.b: Stolen things (res furtivae) were excluded from usucapion by the Twelve Tables and the lex Atinia, until the vice was purged by return to the owner.

cards.f: What two elements make up possession?
cards.b: Corpus (physical control) and animus (intention to hold the thing as one's own).

cards.f: Contrast the interdicts uti possidetis and utrubi.
cards.b: Uti possidetis protected the current possessor of land not holding it by force, stealth or permission from the opponent; utrubi gave movables to whoever had possessed longer in the past year (in classical law).

cards.f: Name Gaius's four categories of contract.
cards.b: Real (re), verbal (verbis), literal (litteris) and consensual (consensu).

cards.f: Name the four consensual contracts.
cards.b: Sale (emptio venditio), hire (locatio conductio), partnership (societas) and mandate (mandatum).

cards.f: Distinguish mutuum from commodatum.
cards.b: Mutuum is a loan for consumption where equivalent goods are returned; commodatum is a gratuitous loan for use where the same thing is returned.

cards.f: What was the stipulatio?
cards.b: An oral contract formed by a question and a matching answer, enforceable regardless of its underlying purpose.

cards.f: What does ex nudo pacto actio non nascitur mean?
cards.b: No action arises from a bare agreement; informal pacts outside the recognised contracts were not generally actionable.

cards.f: When did risk pass to the buyer in Roman sale?
cards.b: When the sale became perfecta, once the thing and price were certain and any conditions satisfied, even before delivery.

cards.f: What remedies did the aediles' edict give a buyer?
cards.b: The actio redhibitoria to rescind the sale and the actio quanti minoris to reduce the price, for latent defects in slaves and animals sold in the market.

cards.f: What were innominate contracts?
cards.b: Reciprocal agreements outside the named contracts, such as exchange, enforceable once one party performed, by the actio praescriptis verbis.

cards.f: What is negotiorum gestio?
cards.b: Managing another's affairs without authority in their interest; it gave rise to reciprocal quasi-contractual obligations.

cards.f: What was the condictio indebiti?
cards.b: An action to recover money or property paid by mistake when it was not owed.

cards.f: Name the three types of locatio conductio.
cards.b: Hire of a thing (rei), hire of services (operarum) and hire of a piece of work (operis).

cards.f: What standard of liability applied to a depositee?
cards.b: Only dolus and gross negligence, because deposit was gratuitous and benefited the depositor.

cards.f: Name Gaius's four delicts.
cards.b: Furtum (theft), rapina (robbery), damnum iniuria datum (wrongful damage) and iniuria (outrage).

cards.f: What did chapter 1 of the lex Aquilia cover?
cards.b: Wrongfully killing another's slave or four-footed herd animal, with damages at the highest value in the preceding year.

cards.f: What did chapter 3 of the lex Aquilia cover?
cards.b: Other damage to property by burning, breaking or rending, with damages based on the value within 30 days, read by the classical jurists as the highest value in the 30 days before the wrong.

cards.f: How did the jurists interpret rumpere in chapter 3?
cards.b: Broadly, as corrumpere (spoiling), so any physical damage to property could fall within it.

cards.f: What does iniuria mean in the lex Aquilia?
cards.b: Unlawfulness, which the jurists interpreted as requiring fault (dolus or culpa).

cards.f: What standard of fault sufficed under the lex Aquilia?
cards.b: Even the slightest fault (levissima culpa) (D.9.2.44 pr.).

cards.f: State the rule in the pruner case (D.9.2.31).
cards.b: A pruner who drops a branch and kills a passer-by is liable if he failed to shout a warning where people might be expected to pass; fault lies in failing to foresee what a diligent person would.

cards.f: State the outcome in the javelin case (D.9.2.9.4).
cards.b: A soldier practising on a training ground who hits a slave is not liable, but someone throwing in a place not meant for it is.

cards.f: What was the corpore corpori requirement?
cards.b: Direct Aquilian liability originally required damage caused by the defendant's body directly to the thing; indirect causation needed an actio in factum.

cards.f: What happened to damages if the defendant denied liability under the lex Aquilia?
cards.b: They doubled (lis infitiando crescit in duplum).

cards.f: How was the barber case (D.9.2.11 pr.) resolved?
cards.b: Where a ball hit a barber's hand and the slave being shaved was cut, liability might fall on the player or barber, but someone who chose to be shaved in a dangerous place had himself to blame.

cards.f: Name two features of Roman penal delictual actions.
cards.b: They were not transmissible against the wrongdoer's heir, and each of several wrongdoers could be sued for the full penalty.

cards.f: Who were the Glossators?
cards.b: Medieval jurists at Bologna, starting with Irnerius, who explained the Digest through marginal and interlinear glosses.

cards.f: What was Accursius's contribution?
cards.b: He compiled the Glossa Ordinaria (about 1230), the standard gloss on the Corpus Iuris Civilis.

cards.f: Who were the Commentators?
cards.b: 14th-century jurists such as Bartolus and Baldus who adapted Roman law to contemporary needs in extended commentaries.

cards.f: What is the ius commune?
cards.b: The combined body of Roman and canon law taught across European universities and used as a common background law.

cards.f: What is the abstraction principle in German law?
cards.b: The real agreement transferring ownership is separate from and valid independently of the underlying obligation, such as a sale.

cards.f: When did the BGB come into force?
cards.b: 1 January 1900.

cards.f: Which French provision contains the general clause on fault liability?
cards.b: Article 1240 of the Code civil (formerly Article 1382).

cards.f: Name four mixed legal systems.
cards.b: Scotland, South Africa, Louisiana and Quebec.

cards.f: How does § 242 BGB contrast with English law?
cards.b: It imposes a general duty of good faith in performance; English law has no general duty and in Walford v Miles [1992] rejected a duty to negotiate in good faith.

cards.f: How did Roman law influence Coggs v Bernard (1703)?
cards.b: Holt CJ drew on Roman categories of bailment, such as deposit and commodatum, to classify bailments and their standards of care.

cards.f: What is jurisprudence constante?
cards.b: The civil law doctrine that a consistent line of decisions carries strong persuasive authority, though not binding as precedent.

cards.f: Which Pandectists shaped the BGB?
cards.b: Notably Savigny, founder of the historical school, and Windscheid, whose textbook on Pandect law was highly influential.

cards.f: What was Junian Latin status?
cards.b: The status of a slave freed informally or without meeting statutory conditions: free, but without citizenship, and unable to make a will, so the estate reverted to the patron on death.

questions.q: Which part of Justinian's Corpus Iuris Civilis consists of excerpts from classical juristic writings?
questions.why: The Digest (533) collects excerpts from jurists such as Ulpian, Paul and Papinian; the Code collects imperial constitutions.

questions.q: Which statute is traditionally said to have made plebiscites binding on all citizens?
questions.why: The lex Hortensia (287 BC) gave plebiscita the force of law for the whole populus.

questions.q: In classical Roman law, patria potestas ended:
options: On the father's death or emancipation
When the son became a citizen
questions.why: Age and marriage did not end potestas; the father's death or emancipation (among a few other events) did.

questions.q: A Roman citizen who adopts a person who is sui iuris does so by:
questions.why: Adrogation applied to persons sui iuris; adoption in the narrow sense applied to persons already in another's power.

questions.q: Which of the following was a res mancipi?
questions.why: Italian land was res mancipi; sheep, provincial land and money were res nec mancipi.

questions.q: Under Justinian's middle view on specificatio, a statue carved from another's marble belongs to:
options: The carver and the owner jointly
The owner of the marble, because it cannot be returned to its original form
The carver, because it cannot be returned to its original form
The owner of the marble in every case
questions.why: If the new thing cannot be reduced to its material, it goes to the maker; a statue cannot be turned back into a block of marble.

questions.q: Which Roman contract was formed by agreement alone?
questions.why: Sale was one of the four consensual contracts; mutuum and commodatum were real, stipulatio verbal.

questions.q: Under a commodatum the borrower must return:
options: Goods of the same kind and quantity
questions.why: Commodatum is a gratuitous loan for use; the same thing is returned. Mutuum requires equivalent goods.

questions.q: Under chapter 1 of the lex Aquilia, damages for killing a slave were measured by:
options: The highest value in the preceding year
The value at the time of death
The value in the following 30 days
questions.why: Chapter 1 used the highest value the slave had in the year before the killing; damages doubled only on wrongful denial.

questions.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes the German BGB from the French Code civil?
options: A general part and the abstraction principle
questions.why: The BGB's abstract General Part and separation of real and obligatory transactions are distinctive Pandectist features.

questions.q: In which case did Holt CJ adopt Roman categories of bailment?
questions.why: Coggs v Bernard (1703) drew on Roman categories such as deposit and commodatum, partly via Bracton.

questions.q: Explain the role of the praetor in the development of Roman law.
markScheme: Urban (367 BC) and peregrine (242 BC) praetors administered justice
Published an annual edict setting out remedies
Could aid, supplement or correct civil law (Papinian, D.1.1.7.1) but not legislate
Created ius honorarium: new actions, exceptiones, bonorum possessio; edict consolidated by Julian c. AD 130
questions.modelAnswer: The urban praetor, from 367 BC, and the peregrine praetor, from 242 BC, controlled access to remedies. Each published an edict stating the actions and defences they would grant. Papinian describes the praetor as aiding, supplementing or correcting the civil law. He could not legislate, but by granting new formulae, exceptiones and remedies such as bonorum possessio he built up the ius honorarium. Under Hadrian the edict was fixed by Julian in about AD 130, ending its creative phase.

questions.q: Explain the legal position of a slave's peculium.
markScheme: Fund the master allowed the slave to manage
Legally owned by the master
Third parties contracting with the slave could sue the master up to its value (actio de peculio)
Allowed slaves to trade and helped commercial life; often used to buy freedom
questions.modelAnswer: A peculium was a fund or property that a master let a slave administer. In law it remained the master's, so the slave owned nothing. It allowed slaves to run businesses, and it mattered commercially because creditors who dealt with the slave could sue the master by the actio de peculio, but only up to the fund's value. Slaves often used their peculium to buy their freedom, and on manumission inter vivos the master might let them keep it.

questions.q: Set out the classical requirements for usucapio and explain why a good faith buyer of a stolen thing could not rely on it.
markScheme: Res habilis: thing capable of usucapion
Iusta causa (titulus)
Good faith at the start of possession
Possession for the period: 1 year movables, 2 years land (Twelve Tables)
Stolen things excluded by Twelve Tables and lex Atinia until return to owner, regardless of buyer's good faith
questions.modelAnswer: Usucapio required a thing capable of usucapion, a recognised cause such as sale or gift, good faith when possession began, and uninterrupted possession for one year for movables or two years for land. Stolen things were excluded by the Twelve Tables and the lex Atinia. The defect attached to the thing, not the person, so even an honest buyer from a thief could not usucapt until the thing had returned to its owner's control.

questions.q: Distinguish the four categories of contract in Gaius.
markScheme: Real: formed by delivery (mutuum, commodatum, depositum, pignus)
Verbal: stipulatio by question and answer
Literal: account book entries
Consensual: agreement alone, good faith (sale, hire, partnership, mandate)
questions.modelAnswer: Gaius classified contracts by how they were formed. Real contracts arose when a thing was delivered, as in mutuum and commodatum. Verbal contracts arose from formal spoken words, chiefly the stipulatio's question and matching answer. Literal contracts arose from entries in account books and had faded by Justinian's time. Consensual contracts (sale, hire, partnership and mandate) arose from agreement alone and were governed by good faith.

questions.q: Calpurnius's slave, a skilled cook, was worth 6,000 sesterces in March but only 4,000 in November after an illness. In December Fabia negligently kills him with her cart. Fabia denies liability and loses. Calculate the damages under chapter 1 of the lex Aquilia, showing your reasoning.
markScheme: Identifies chapter 1: killing a slave
Fault (culpa) suffices as iniuria
Highest value in the year before death: 6,000
March is within the preceding year
Denial doubles damages
Total 12,000 sesterces
questions.modelAnswer: Killing a slave falls under chapter 1. Fabia's negligence is culpa, which counts as iniuria. Damages are the highest value the slave had in the year before his death. March falls within that year, so the measure is 6,000 sesterces, not the 4,000 he was worth when killed. Because Fabia denied liability and lost, damages double: 6,000 × 2 = 12,000 sesterces.

questions.q: Briefly explain how Roman law was received in medieval and early modern Europe.
markScheme: Rediscovery of the Digest in late 11th-century Italy
Glossators at Bologna (Irnerius, Accursius)
Commentators (Bartolus, Baldus) adapted it to practice
Ius commune with canon law; later humanism and natural law; codification
questions.modelAnswer: The Digest re-emerged in Italy in the late 11th century. At Bologna, Irnerius and the Glossators explained it; Accursius's Glossa Ordinaria (about 1230) became the standard gloss. The Commentators, such as Bartolus and Baldus, adapted Roman law to contemporary needs. Combined with canon law, it formed the ius commune taught across Europe. Humanists and natural lawyers later reorganised it, and it fed into the great codes such as the Code civil and BGB.

questions.q: Explain the difference between possession and ownership in Roman law, with an example.
markScheme: Ownership (dominium) is the fullest right, protected by rei vindicatio
Possession is factual control with intention (corpus and animus), protected by interdicts regardless of title
Example: a thief possesses but does not own; tenant has only detention
questions.modelAnswer: Ownership was the fullest right over a thing and was protected by the rei vindicatio. Possession was factual control combined with the intention to hold as one's own. It was protected by interdicts regardless of title, keeping the peace until ownership was decided. A thief possessed but did not own, and could use interdicts against third parties. A tenant, holding for the owner, had only detention.

questions.q: Compare classical Roman marriage with and without manus.
markScheme: With manus: wife entered husband's family, under his power, as if a daughter
Created by confarreatio, coemptio or usus; rare by classical period
Without manus: wife remained in father's power or sui iuris; property separate; gifts between spouses void
Dowry and free divorce
questions.modelAnswer: In marriage with manus the wife passed into her husband's power, or his father's, and stood as a daughter for inheritance purposes, with her property going to the husband. It arose by confarreatio, coemptio or usus and was rare by the classical period. In marriage without manus, the norm, the wife stayed in her father's power or was independent. Property remained separate, gifts between spouses were void, a dowry was usual, and either spouse could divorce.

questions.q: What is the rule ex nudo pacto actio non nascitur?
markScheme: No action arises from a bare agreement
Only agreements fitting a recognised contract (or enforced pacts) were actionable
questions.modelAnswer: It means no action arises from a bare pact. An informal agreement that did not fit one of the recognised contracts (real, verbal, literal or consensual) was not actionable in itself. It could be enforced only if it fell within a category of pact that the praetor or later imperial law chose to enforce, or was attached to a good faith contract.

questions.q: Why must Romanists be cautious when using the Digest as evidence of classical law?
markScheme: Compiled in 530–533 from earlier works
Compilers authorised to alter texts; interpolations
Texts shortened and taken out of context
Need to compare other sources, e.g. Gaius's Institutes (Verona palimpsest)
questions.modelAnswer: The Digest was compiled from classical writings between 530 and 533. Justinian authorised the compilers to cut and change texts to bring them into line with contemporary law, so some passages contain interpolations. Excerpts are also taken out of context and shortened. Scholars therefore compare independent sources, especially Gaius's Institutes, recovered from the Verona palimpsest. Modern scholarship is more cautious about detecting interpolations than earlier critics were.

questions.q: Lucilla is pruning a tall tree beside a public path in her vineyard. Without warning she lets a heavy branch fall, which strikes and kills Gaius's slave Stichus, who was walking along the path. The same afternoon, Quintus, practising javelin throwing in his own field, hits and wounds Gaius's horse, which had strayed through a broken fence. Advise Gaius on his claims under the lex Aquilia.
markScheme: Identifies chapter 1 for killing Stichus (slave)
Damnum: loss to Gaius as owner; highest value in past year
Iniuria requires fault; levissima culpa suffices
Pruner case (D.9.2.31): liability where no warning given near a public path
Paul's test: failing to foresee what a diligent person would foresee
Lucilla's direct causation corpore corpori satisfied
Horse wound is chapter 3 (damage, not killing) — horse is pecus but not killed
Javelin case (D.9.2.9.4): throwing in a proper place is not culpable; consider whether field is appropriate
Gaius's own fault in letting horse stray may defeat or reduce claim
Doubling on denial; reasoned advice
questions.modelAnswer:
Stichus. Killing a slave falls within chapter 1. Gaius suffered loss as owner and may claim the highest value Stichus had in the year before his death. The key issue is iniuria, which the jurists read as requiring fault, though even the slightest fault is enough. The pruner case (D.9.2.31) is directly in point. A pruner who drops a branch is liable if she fails to call out a warning where people may be passing, especially near a public path. Paul defines culpa as failing to foresee what a diligent person could have foreseen. Lucilla was working beside a public path and gave no warning, so she was at fault. Causation is direct: the branch she released struck Stichus, satisfying corpore corpori. Gaius has a strong claim, and if Lucilla denies liability and loses, damages will be doubled.

The horse. A horse is a four-footed herd animal, but because it was wounded rather than killed, the claim falls under chapter 3, as damage to property. The measure is based on the value within 30 days, which the classical jurists read as the highest value in the 30 days before the wrong.

Liability turns on fault. In the javelin case (D.9.2.9.4) a soldier practising on a designated training ground is not liable if he hits a slave crossing it, whereas someone throwing in an unsuitable place is. Quintus was in his own field, a place where throwing is arguably legitimate, and the horse entered through a broken fence. Unless Quintus saw the horse, or should have expected animals there, he is likely not at fault. If the fence was Gaius's responsibility, his own carelessness further weakens the claim; Roman jurists recognised that a victim's fault could defeat liability, as in the barber case.

Advice: Gaius should sue Lucilla under chapter 1 with good prospects. His claim against Quintus is weak unless he can show Quintus was careless in the circumstances.

questions.q: Marcia agrees with Decimus to sell him her slave Eros for 5,000 sesterces. They agree on the slave and the price, and Decimus pays 1,000 as a deposit. Before delivery, Eros dies of a fever that Marcia could not have prevented. Separately, Marcia lends her neighbour Titia a silver dish for a banquet, without charge; Titia's guest steals it. Marcia also informally promised her nephew 2,000 sesterces as a gift, but now refuses to pay. Advise the parties under classical Roman law.
markScheme: Sale is consensual, perfect on agreement of thing and price
Risk passes on perfection: periculum est emptoris
Decimus must pay the remaining 4,000 if Marcia not at fault
Marcia liable only if fault or if she had assumed custodia/was in mora
Lending the dish free is commodatum (real contract)
Commodatarius liable for custodia, including theft by third party
Titia liable to Marcia via actio commodati; Titia may have an action against the thief
Gift promise: bare pact, no action (ex nudo pacto)
Would be enforceable if made by stipulatio (and note lex Cincia limits on gifts)
Clear, reasoned conclusions on each issue
questions.modelAnswer:
Sale of Eros. Sale was a consensual contract, formed by agreement on the thing and the price. Here both were certain and there were no conditions, so the sale was perfect. On perfection risk passed to the buyer: periculum est emptoris. Eros died of illness without Marcia's fault and before she was in delay over delivery. Decimus therefore bears the loss. He cannot recover his 1,000 and remains liable for the remaining 4,000 (5,000 − 1,000). Marcia would be liable only if the death resulted from her failure to take proper care, or if she had delayed delivery after it was due.

The silver dish. Lending a thing for use without payment is commodatum, a real contract formed by delivery. The borrower must return the same thing. Because commodatum benefited the borrower, the classical standard was high, including custodia, meaning liability for loss through theft even without fault. Titia is therefore liable to Marcia under the actio commodati for the dish's value, even though the thief was a guest. Having been held liable, Titia has the interest needed to bring the actio furti against the thief. Liability would not extend to irresistible force such as robbery by armed bandits.

The promised gift. Marcia's informal promise was a bare pact. Roman law gave no action on it: ex nudo pacto actio non nascitur. The nephew cannot enforce it. Had it been made by stipulatio, a formal question and answer, it would have been actionable, subject to the restrictions of the lex Cincia (204 BC) on large gifts, whose exact limits are uncertain.

Conclusion: Decimus bears the risk of Eros's death; Titia is liable for the dish; the nephew has no claim.

questions.q: Sempronius finds a wild boar wounded by Flavius's spear in a forest and captures it. He takes it to his estate, where it escapes back into the forest a week later. Meanwhile, Sempronius's tenant builds a shed on Sempronius's land using timber belonging to Aulus, and Sempronius's slave makes wine from grapes belonging to Cornelia. Advise on the ownership of the boar, the shed and the wine.
markScheme: Wild animals are res nullius, acquired by occupatio
Wounding not enough: ownership only on capture (J.2.1.13); Sempronius acquires
Ownership lost when animal regains natural freedom; boar becomes ownerless again
Shed: superficies solo cedit; building accedes to the land (Sempronius)
Timber owner cannot vindicate while built in (Twelve Tables tignum iunctum); actio de tigno iuncto for double value
Can vindicate if building is taken down
Wine from grapes: specificatio
Justinian's middle view: wine cannot be reduced to grapes, so maker's owner (Sempronius via slave) takes, if in good faith
Cornelia's remedies (e.g. condictio or actio furti if bad faith)
Reasoned conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
The boar. Wild animals are ownerless and become the property of whoever captures them (occupatio). Justinian's Institutes (J.2.1.13) settle the controversy over wounded animals: wounding alone gives no ownership, which arises only on capture, since many things may prevent the hunter from catching the animal. Flavius therefore acquired nothing by wounding the boar, and Sempronius became owner on capture. Ownership of a wild animal lasts only while it is kept under control. When it escapes and regains its natural freedom, it becomes ownerless again, available to the next person who catches it.

The shed. Under superficies solo cedit, whatever is built on land accedes to the land. The shed belongs to Sempronius as landowner, not to the tenant or Aulus. The Twelve Tables prevented the owner of timber built into a structure from claiming it back while it stayed in place (tignum iunctum), to avoid demolition. Aulus instead had the actio de tigno iuncto for double the value against the person who built it in. If the shed is later taken down, Aulus may vindicate his timber.

The wine. Making wine from another's grapes is specificatio. The Sabinians gave the product to the owner of the material, the Proculians to the maker. Justinian adopted a middle view. If the new thing can be reduced to its original material, the material owner takes it. If not, the maker does. Wine cannot be turned back into grapes, so the wine belongs to the maker. A slave acquires for his master, so Sempronius owns it. Justinian's rule assumed the maker acted in good faith. If the slave knowingly used stolen grapes, Cornelia could bring the actio furti and a condictio. In any case she should have a claim for the value of her grapes.

questions.q: 'Patria potestas made Roman family law a law of property in persons.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines patria potestas and its lifelong duration
Ius vitae necisque in early law and its decline
Children in power owned nothing; acquisitions to the father
Parallel with slavery: peculium, actio de peculio
Creation by birth, adoption, adrogation; ending by emancipation via three sales
Countervailing features: filius familias as citizen with public rights; could hold office and marry
Development of peculium castrense and quasi-castrense
Imperial limits on paternal power (e.g. exposure, harsh punishment)
Marriage without manus and wife's independence
Evaluation of the proposition with nuance
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Patria potestas was the power of the paterfamilias over his descendants through males. Gaius regarded it as peculiar to Roman citizens. It lasted for life, ending only with the father's death, emancipation or a few special events, so a 50-year-old consul could still be in his father's power.

Several features support the proposition. In early law the father had ius vitae necisque, the power of life and death. Children in power could own nothing in civil law; whatever they acquired went to the father. They might hold a peculium, which in law was the father's, and third parties could sue the father by the actio de peculio, exactly as for slaves. Emancipation used the Twelve Tables rule that a father who sold his son three times lost potestas, treating the son as an object of sale. The father could also give a son in noxal surrender for wrongs the son committed.

The proposition overstates matters, though. A son in power was a free citizen. He could vote, hold magistracies and serve in the army, and in public law he was fully a person. Marriage needed his consent as well as his father's. The power of life and death was rarely used and was eroded in the Empire. Fathers who killed sons without a hearing could be punished, and emperors restricted exposure and harsh treatment. From Augustus, sons gained the peculium castrense, property earned through military service that they could dispose of freely, extended later to the peculium quasi-castrense for earnings in public service. Justinian further limited paternal rights over property from the mother's side.

Wives were increasingly outside the scheme. By the classical period marriage without manus was usual, so a wife was not in her husband's power and kept her property.

The better view is that potestas was a concentration of patrimonial and disciplinary authority in one head of household, used to keep family property together. It had property-like features, especially early on, but citizenship marked a firm line between children and slaves, and later law softened paternal power considerably.

questions.q: Assess the significance of the formulary system and the praetor's edict for the creativity of classical Roman law.
markScheme: Contrasts legis actiones: rigid oral forms
Formulary procedure: lex Aebutia and leges Iuliae; two stages before praetor and iudex
Structure of formula: intentio, condemnatio, demonstratio, exceptio
Flexibility: new formulae, actiones in factum, fictions, exceptions
Bonae fidei iudicia allowing good faith considerations (consensual contracts)
Praetor's role to aid, supplement, correct (Papinian); ius honorarium
Examples: exceptio doli, bonorum possessio, actio Publiciana
Jurists' role in drafting and interpreting formulae
Julian's consolidation c. AD 130 and shift to cognitio
Evaluation: procedure-driven development; limits (no general contract)
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Early Roman procedure under the legis actiones was rigid. Claims had to be made in fixed oral forms, and Gaius records that a litigant who said 'vines' instead of 'trees', as the Twelve Tables required, lost his case. The formulary system, introduced by the lex Aebutia and made general by Augustus's leges Iuliae, changed this.

In the first stage, before the praetor, the parties agreed a written formula. In the second, a lay iudex heard evidence and decided. The formula had standard parts: the intentio stating the claim, the condemnatio empowering the judge to condemn or absolve, and where needed a demonstratio or exceptio. This structure gave the praetor great scope. He could draft new formulae, grant actions in factum based on facts rather than civil-law rights, use fictions (such as treating a non-citizen as a citizen), and insert defences.

Papinian's description of the praetor as aiding, supplementing and correcting the civil law captures the result: the ius honorarium. The exceptio doli let defendants resist claims brought in bad faith. The actio Publiciana protected bonitary owners as if usucapion were complete. Bonorum possessio reshaped succession. In the bonae fidei iudicia, the formula directed the judge to award whatever good faith required, letting the consensual contracts develop flexibly.

The jurists were central. They advised praetors and parties, drafted model formulae and interpreted the edict, which is why so much of the Digest is commentary on it.

The system also had limits. Development was remedy-led rather than principle-led, so Roman law never reached a general law of contract or delict. After Julian consolidated the edict in about AD 130, praetorian creativity largely ceased. Under the cognitio, imperial officials and rescripts took over development.

Overall, the formulary system and the edict were the main engines of classical creativity. They turned the narrow ius civile into a flexible body of law, while leaving a casuistic structure that later systematisers had to reorganise.

questions.q: 'The civil law and common law traditions differ less in substance than in method and style.' Discuss with reference to contract and delict.
markScheme: Outlines the shared Roman roots and reception (ius commune, Coggs v Bernard)
Method: deductive code-based vs inductive precedent
Role of doctrine in civil law and of judges in common law
Jurisprudence constante vs stare decisis; convergence in practice
Contract: consideration vs cause/no requirement
Contract: specific performance primary in civil law vs damages in England
Contract: good faith (§ 242 BGB) vs Walford v Miles; partial convergence
Third-party rights: stipulation pour autrui vs privity and 1999 Act
Delict: French general clause (art 1240) vs German protected interests (§ 823) vs English nominate torts
Pure economic loss restrictions in both England and Germany
Conclusion weighing substance vs method
questions.modelAnswer:
Both traditions share Roman roots. Roman law was received on the Continent through the ius commune and also influenced English law through Bracton and cases such as Coggs v Bernard (1703).

Method clearly differs. Civil law reasons from codes and general principles, aided by influential academic doctrine. Common law develops inductively from cases under stare decisis. Even here convergence exists: civil courts follow jurisprudence constante, and English law is now heavily statutory.

Substance differs too, though often less than labels suggest. In contract, English law requires consideration or a deed, while civil systems do not. Yet the practical difference is small, since doctrines such as promissory estoppel soften consideration. Civil law treats specific performance as a primary remedy; English law treats damages as primary and specific performance as discretionary. In practice civil-law claimants often prefer damages. Good faith marks a real difference. Section 242 BGB imposes a general duty of good faith, whereas Walford v Miles [1992] 2 AC 128 rejected a duty to negotiate in good faith. English courts have found implied duties in some relational contracts, but no general principle. On third-party rights, the civilian stipulation pour autrui long contrasted with privity, but the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 has narrowed the gap.

In delict, civil systems themselves differ. French law has a broad general clause in Article 1240 of the Code civil, close to the Roman Aquilian idea of liability for fault. German law in § 823 BGB protects listed interests, such as life, body, health, freedom and property, and is more restrictive. English law has a set of nominate torts, with negligence as a general category since Donoghue v Stevenson. English and German law both restrict recovery for pure economic loss, while French law is more generous. So the main substantive divide in delict runs through the civil law family, not between traditions.

The proposition is largely right. Many differences are of method and style, and functional outcomes often converge. But genuine substantive differences remain, notably consideration, good faith and remedies, and grouping all civil systems together hides important internal variety.

questions.q: 'The Roman law of delict under the lex Aquilia developed from a narrow, almost penal statute into a general principle of liability for fault.' Critically evaluate this claim, and assess its influence on modern civilian systems.
markScheme: Context: plebiscite c. 287 BC; three chapters; penal features
Narrow original scope: killing slaves and pecus; urere, frangere, rumpere
Penal elements: highest past value, doubling on denial, non-transmissibility
Interpretive widening: rumpere as corrumpere
Iniuria reinterpreted as fault, levissima culpa; Paul's foreseeability test in pruner case
Damnum as id quod interest, including consequential loss
Causation: corpore corpori and extension by actiones in factum and utiles
Extension to non-owners and free persons (D.9.2.13)
Limits: still tied to property damage; casuistry; no full general clause in Roman law
Ius commune and natural lawyers (Grotius) generalised it; French art 1240; South African Aquilian action
German § 823 as a more restrictive heir
Critical conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The lex Aquilia, traditionally dated to 287 BC, began narrowly. Chapter 1 covered killing another's slave or four-footed herd animal. Chapter 3 covered burning, breaking or rending other property. It had penal features: damages measured by the highest value in a past period could exceed the actual loss, liability doubled on denial, and the action did not lie against the wrongdoer's heir.

The jurists widened it in several ways. They read rumpere as corrumpere, covering any spoiling of property. They interpreted iniuria not merely as unlawfulness but as requiring fault, holding that even the slightest fault sufficed (D.9.2.44 pr.). In the pruner case Paul explained culpa as failing to foresee what a diligent person could have foreseen, a recognisably modern negligence test. Damnum came to mean the owner's financial interest, allowing recovery of consequential loss. The original requirement of direct bodily harm to the thing was supplemented by actiones in factum and utiles for indirect causation. Protection extended to non-owners such as usufructuaries, and Ulpian reports an actio utilis for a free person injured (D.9.2.13 pr.).

The claim therefore has substance, but it should be qualified. Roman law never adopted a general clause. Liability remained structured by the statute's categories and by casuistic extensions. It was centred on damage to property and on physical harm. Penal elements survived into Justinian's law. Insults and injury to personality fell under the separate delict of iniuria.

The decisive generalisation came later. Medieval jurists, the usus modernus and natural lawyers such as Grotius, who stated a general duty to repair loss caused by fault, removed the penal features and abstracted a principle. This fed into Article 1382 of the French Code civil, now Article 1240, with its broad clause of fault liability. South African law still speaks of the Aquilian action for patrimonial loss caused wrongfully and culpably. German law took a more restrictive path, with § 823 BGB listing protected interests, reflecting Pandectist caution.

Conclusion: the lex Aquilia moved a long way towards fault-based liability through juristic interpretation. Its transformation into a general principle, however, was largely the work of its later reception.

questions.q: 'Roman law never had a law of contract, only a law of contracts.' Critically evaluate this statement and consider whether it remains true of the modern civil law.
markScheme: Explains the contrast: closed list of contracts vs general principle
Gaius's fourfold classification and the specific contracts
Bare pacts unenforceable: ex nudo pacto
Stipulatio as a near-general instrument for any lawful promise
Consensual contracts and good faith as a unifying principle
Innominate contracts and actio praescriptis verbis widened enforceability
Pacta praetoria and legitima; pacta adiecta in good faith contracts
Labeo's and others' discussions of agreement (conventio) as a common element (Pedius/Ulpian D.2.14.1.3)
Medieval and canonist move to pacta sunt servanda; natural lawyers
Modern codes: general contract law (e.g. French Code civil after 2016; BGB general part)
Evaluation: partial truth; development and modern position
Clear conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement captures a real feature of Roman law. There was no general rule that agreements were binding. The Romans recognised specific contracts, which Gaius classified by how they arose. Real contracts were formed by delivery, verbal contracts by formal words, literal contracts by entries in accounts, and consensual contracts by agreement. Outside these categories, the rule was ex nudo pacto actio non nascitur: a bare pact gave no action.

The statement nevertheless needs qualification. First, the stipulatio worked as an almost general tool. Any lawful promise could be made binding by putting it into question-and-answer form. Second, the consensual contracts and other bonae fidei iudicia shared a common principle of good faith, which allowed judges to develop general rules. Third, the innominate contracts, such as exchange, became enforceable by the actio praescriptis verbis once one party had performed, filling many gaps. Fourth, certain pacts were enforced by the praetor or by imperial law, and informal pacts attached to good faith contracts were also enforced. Finally, the jurists recognised agreement as a unifying idea. Ulpian reports Pedius's view that there is no contract and no obligation that does not involve agreement (D.2.14.1.3).

The move to a general law of contract came after Rome. Canon lawyers held that every serious promise should be kept, giving rise to the maxim pacta sunt servanda. Natural lawyers such as Grotius built a general theory around promise and consent. The modern codes adopted this approach. The French Code civil, especially after the 2016 reform, sets out general rules on formation, validity and effects of contracts, with the specific contracts treated separately. The BGB treats contract under its General Part as a kind of juristic act and builds a general law of obligations. Named contracts survive, but as specialised regimes within a general law.

Conclusion: the statement is broadly true of Roman law's structure, though Roman law contained the tools and principles for generalisation. It is no longer true of the modern civil law, which has a general law of contract while keeping a Roman-inspired law of specific contracts.

questions.q: Domitius sells and delivers (but does not mancipate) an Italian farm to Valeria in 120 AD. Eighteen months later, Domitius dies and his heir Lucius claims the farm from Valeria by rei vindicatio. At the same time, Valeria discovers that a horse she bought in good faith from a market trader eleven months ago had been stolen from Petronius, who now demands it. Advise Valeria.
markScheme: Italian land is res mancipi; mancipatio or in iure cessio needed for civil-law ownership
Traditio alone gives bonitary ownership (in bonis)
Valeria can usucapt in two years for land; after 18 months not yet complete
Lucius has civil-law title (quiritary ownership) as heir
Praetor protects Valeria: exceptio rei venditae et traditae against seller and heir
Actio Publiciana available to Valeria against third parties
After 6 more months she becomes full owner by usucapion
Horse: res nec mancipi but stolen; usucapion barred (Twelve Tables, lex Atinia)
Good faith buyer cannot resist Petronius's vindicatio; no market overt rule
Valeria's remedy against seller for eviction (warranty against eviction / actio empti)
Clear, reasoned advice
questions.modelAnswer:
The farm. Italian land was res mancipi, so civil-law ownership could pass only by mancipatio or in iure cessio. Domitius merely delivered it, so Valeria did not become civil-law owner. Domitius kept bare quiritary title, which passed to his heir Lucius. However, Valeria received the land under a valid sale with delivery and acquired bonitary ownership (in bonis). The praetor protected this. If Lucius brings the rei vindicatio, Valeria can raise the exceptio rei venditae et traditae, the defence that the thing was sold and delivered. This operates against the seller and his heir, so Lucius's claim fails. Against third parties Valeria can use the actio Publiciana, which treats her as if usucapion were complete.

Usucapion will also cure her title. The period for land was two years. After 18 months she has six months to go. Once it is complete she will be full civil-law owner, and Lucius's bare title will end. The heir takes over the deceased's position, so Domitius's death does not interrupt Valeria's possession.

The horse. Horses were res nec mancipi, so delivery could transfer ownership, but only from an owner. The trader was not owner, so Valeria acquired no ownership. Usucapion would normally take one year for movables, and she has possessed for eleven months. But stolen things could not be usucapted, under the Twelve Tables and the lex Atinia, until the defect was purged by return to the owner. Her good faith does not help. Roman law had no rule protecting buyers in open markets. Petronius can vindicate the horse.

Valeria's remedy lies against the trader. A seller warranted the buyer against eviction, so once Petronius recovers the horse she can sue on the sale (actio empti) for her loss, or on any stipulation for double the price if one was made. If the trader knew the horse was stolen, he is also liable for theft.

Advice: Valeria keeps the farm; she must return the horse and sue the trader.

questions.q: Explain the contribution of the Glossators and Commentators to the formation of the civil law tradition.
markScheme: Rediscovery of the Digest in 11th-century Italy (Littera Florentina)
Irnerius and the Bologna school
Method of glossing: explanation, cross-reference, harmonising contradictions
Accursius's Glossa Ordinaria (c. 1230) and its authority
Commentators: Bartolus and Baldus; adaptation to practice and statuta
Conflict of laws and other new doctrines
Formation of the ius commune with canon law
Spread through universities and trained jurists
Evaluation of their legacy
questions.modelAnswer:
The Digest re-emerged in Italy in the late 11th century, most famously through the manuscript later known as the Littera Florentina. At Bologna, Irnerius began teaching it, founding the school of the Glossators. Their method was close textual study. They wrote glosses between the lines and in the margins to explain terms, cross-refer to other passages and reconcile apparent contradictions. They treated Justinian's texts as authoritative and complete, a kind of written reason.

Accursius's Glossa Ordinaria, compiled in about 1230, gathered this work into a standard apparatus. It became so authoritative that courts often followed the gloss rather than the text itself.

The Commentators, active in the 14th century, included Bartolus of Sassoferrato and Baldus de Ubaldis. They wrote fuller commentaries aimed at practice and gave legal opinions (consilia). They adapted Roman law to the needs of Italian city-states, reconciling it with local statutes and feudal and canon law. Bartolus helped develop the theory of conflict of laws, working out how statutes applied to foreigners and to property in different cities.

Together with the canonists, they formed the ius commune, a shared European legal science taught in universities from Italy to Germany, Spain, France and beyond. Graduates staffed courts and chanceries, spreading the learned law into local practice. This explains why later systems share vocabulary, concepts and methods.

Their legacy is both a body of doctrine and a style: systematic, text-based, and confident that law could be reasoned from authoritative sources. Humanists later criticised them for distorting texts, but the codes of the 19th century still rest on the concepts they developed.

questions.q: Publius, a Roman citizen aged 40, lives in the household of his father Aurelius. Publius has served as a soldier and saved 10,000 sesterces from his army pay. He also runs a bakery with a fund Aurelius allowed him to manage, and owes a miller 3,000 sesterces for flour. Publius's slave Felix, aged 25, was freed by Publius informally among friends last year. Aurelius has just died. Advise on (a) who owned Publius's savings and the bakery fund before Aurelius's death, (b) the miller's position, and (c) Felix's status.
markScheme: Publius in patria potestas despite age 40; potestas lasts until father's death
Military savings are peculium castrense: Publius could hold and dispose of them
Bakery fund is ordinary peculium (profecticium), legally Aurelius's
Miller could sue Aurelius by actio de peculio up to the fund's value (or quod iussu/institoria if authorised)
On Aurelius's death Publius becomes sui iuris and paterfamilias
Publius now personally liable and owns property in his own right (subject to inheritance)
Can a son in power manumit? Slave in ordinary peculium belongs to father; consider authority
Informal manumission gives at most Junian Latin status, not citizenship
Lex Aelia Sentia: slave under 30 cannot become citizen by formal manumission without cause shown
Reasoned advice
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Although Publius is 40, he was in his father's power until Aurelius died, because age did not end patria potestas. In civil law a son in power owned nothing, and his acquisitions went to the father. There were exceptions. Property earned through military service formed the peculium castrense, which the son could hold and dispose of as if he were independent. Publius's 10,000 sesterces of army savings were therefore his. The bakery fund was an ordinary peculium. Aurelius allowed Publius to manage it, but in law it belonged to Aurelius.

(b) While Aurelius lived, the miller who sold flour to Publius for the bakery could sue Aurelius by the actio de peculio up to the value of the fund. If Aurelius had authorised the trade or appointed Publius to run the business, wider actions, such as the actio institoria, might make him fully liable. Publius himself could be sued, since sons in power were capable of being bound by contract, though enforcing judgment against him was difficult while he owned nothing. Now that Aurelius has died, Publius is sui iuris and can be sued and held liable from his own property.

(c) Felix's status is doubtful. If Felix was part of the bakery peculium or otherwise belonged to Aurelius, Publius, as a son in power, could not free him without his father's authority. Even assuming valid authority, an informal manumission among friends did not make a slave a citizen. At most it gave Junian Latin status: Felix would be free but without citizenship or the right to make a will. In addition, under the lex Aelia Sentia, a slave under 30 could not become a citizen by manumission unless cause was shown before a council. To give Felix citizenship, Publius, now independent and owning Felix, should free him formally, for example by vindicta before a magistrate, after showing cause.
